strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating whether machine unlearning actually removes information rather than merely causing misclassification.

The core observation that misclassified forget examples may still retain high model confidence or appear in uncertainty sets is useful, and the paper makes a reasonable attempt to expose this via conformal prediction sets.

The empirical section compares several unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, includes random and class-wise forgetting settings, and reports multiple alpha values and standard deviations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central CR metric is not sound as an unlearning measure. Because CR divides coverage by set size, it can be made small by producing very large prediction sets, even when the true forget label remains included. The class-wise Tiny ImageNet results illustrate this degeneracy: RT has coverage near 1 and set size near 200 on forget data, yet CR is near 0 and is interpreted as successful forgetting.

The proposed optimization loss appears mathematically sign-inverted. With S(x,y)=1-p_y and prediction sets defined by S<=q, excluding the true label requires S(true)>q. However Eq. 8 defines L_unlearn=max(S(true)-q,-Delta) and says it is minimized, whose optimum is S(true)<=q-Delta, explicitly keeping the true label inside the conformal set. This undermines the claimed mechanism of the framework.

The paper does not establish that conformal prediction-set exclusion corresponds to removal of training-data influence, privacy, or legal unlearning. The metrics mostly measure confidence/calibration behavior, not closeness to a retrained model or deletion of memorized information.

The evaluation is vulnerable to calibration distribution issues. The authors acknowledge that label-corruption methods shift the forget distribution away from the calibration distribution, but the proposed shadow/semi-shadow adjustment is ad hoc and not integrated into the main metric definition or validated rigorously.

The empirical gains of the proposed framework are mainly improvements on the authors' own metric and UA, with limited evidence against stronger privacy/membership, memorization, or retraining-equivalence criteria. The method is only applied to RT/FT/RL rather than the stronger set of baselines used in metric evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code link, seed protocol, detailed unlearning hyperparameters for all baselines, compute budget, or enough implementation detail to confidently reproduce the many baseline comparisons.

The limitations and ethics discussion are inadequate. The impact statement is generic despite the paper making privacy- and GDPR-related claims, and it does not discuss risks of overclaiming unlearning guarantees from confidence-based metrics.

Presentation has numerous clarity and correctness issues, including inconsistent terminology, typos, confusing metric directions, and tables where the interpretation of gaps and absolute values is hard to follow. These issues make it difficult to verify the claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a real weakness of common unlearning evaluations: simple unlearning accuracy and MIA summaries can hide cases where the forgotten example's true label remains plausible under the model. This is a useful diagnostic direction.

The empirical scope is broader than a toy study: the manuscript evaluates multiple unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, includes random and class-wise forgetting, reports some standard deviations, and studies several alpha values.
The paper is generally readable and the motivation is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central metric is not well justified as a measure of unlearning. CR = coverage / set size can be reduced by making prediction sets very large, so it often rewards uncertainty rather than deletion of information. This is especially visible in class-wise forgetting where retraining can have prediction sets of size 10 or 200 with coverage near 1, yielding tiny CR values that are treated as good forgetting despite including the true forgotten class.

The conformal prediction framing is statistically weak. The paper explicitly notes that exchangeability may not hold in unlearning settings, but then uses conformal-style sets as if they provide reliable evidence of forgetting. The proposed metrics inherit sensitivity to calibration distribution, alpha, and set-size artifacts, and the paper does not provide a rigorous argument connecting them to removal of training-data influence.

The proposed unlearning loss appears internally inconsistent. With S(x,y)=1-p_y, Eq. 8 minimizes max(S(x,y_t)-q, -Delta), which encourages S <= q-Delta, i.e. higher true-label probability and inclusion in the prediction set. This is the opposite of the stated goal of excluding the true label, and directly contradicts the claimed analogy to the C&W loss.

The empirical claims are not convincing enough to support acceptance. Improvements from the framework are often modest and trade off against utility; for example CIFAR-10 RT at alpha=0.1 changes CR_Df from 0.943 to 0.879 at lambda=0.5 while UA rises only from 8.6% to 14.0%. Tiny ImageNet/RL has large variance and degraded accuracy. The paper does not establish that the method improves true unlearning rather than manipulating the proposed metric.

The use of 'RT' is confusing and potentially misleading. Retraining is normally the gold-standard model trained without forget data, but the proposed framework is also applied to RT using forget data in the unlearning loss. This blurs the baseline and raises questions about whether the procedure is a valid post-deletion unlearning method.

The evaluation omits important unlearning evidence: no comparison to exact retrain distributions beyond metric gaps, no privacy attack suite beyond the described MIA variant, no auditing of retained memorization, and no statistical test that improvements are meaningful. Grad-CAM examples are anecdotal and do not substantiate forgetting.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives some training settings, but baseline-specific hyperparameters, unlearning schedules, exact splits, calibration construction details, and code are not sufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Several tables and descriptions contain typos or inconsistencies, which further lowers confidence.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. For a privacy-relevant topic, the paper should be much more explicit about what the metrics do not guarantee, how conformal-set exclusion can be gamed, and why the approach should not be interpreted as certified data removal.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in machine unlearning evaluation: accuracy-style metrics can miss cases where the forgotten label remains plausible under uncertainty. This is a useful and timely observation for privacy-oriented evaluation.

The empirical study is fairly broad for the setting considered, covering random and class-wise forgetting, CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, ResNet-18 and ViT, multiple unlearning baselines, several alpha values, and repeated trials with standard deviations in the appendix.

The proposed use of prediction sets as a diagnostic is intuitive, and the tables showing misclassified forget examples still appearing in conformal sets provide concrete evidence that UA and MIA alone are incomplete.
The paper includes some reproducibility details, including training epochs, optimizer, learning rates, batch size, calibration sizes, alpha values, and lambda values.
weaknesses: The central metric is not fully convincing. CR is defined as coverage divided by set size, so a method can obtain a low forget-data CR by producing very large prediction sets, even if the true label is almost always included. This conflates uncertainty, forgetting, and degraded calibration in a way that weakens the claim that low CR means better unlearning.

The conformal-prediction motivation is technically underdeveloped. The paper acknowledges that exchangeability may fail in unlearning settings, but then largely proceeds as if conformal sets provide meaningful evidence of forgetting. More theory or controlled calibration analysis is needed to justify the interpretation.

There appears to be a serious sign/objective inconsistency in the proposed loss. With S(x,y)=1-p_y, minimizing Lunlearn=max(S(x,yt)-q,-Delta) seems to push S below q, which would make the true label more likely to remain in the conformal set, contrary to the stated goal of forgetting. This makes the method description difficult to trust without clarification.

The method evaluation is limited to applying the framework to RT, FT, and RL, despite the paper presenting it as a general training-based unlearning framework. Stronger baselines, broader integration, and clearer ablations against simpler confidence-suppression losses are needed.

Presentation has several issues: dense and hard-to-read tables, inconsistent wording, typos, and some confusing claims about whether larger or smaller prediction sets indicate better forgetting. These do not invalidate the idea but reduce confidence in the technical details.

Reproducibility is only partial: no code or implementation source is provided, details for individual unlearning baselines and MIA construction are sparse, and the calibration/shadow-model procedures would be hard to reproduce exactly.

The ethics/impact discussion is too generic for a privacy and unlearning paper. It should discuss risks such as false confidence in deletion guarantees, misuse of weak metrics for compliance claims, and limitations of empirical unlearning evaluation.

strengths: The paper identifies a real evaluation concern in machine unlearning: common metrics such as forget-set accuracy and MIA can be too coarse, and uncertainty-aware evaluation is a worthwhile direction.
The manuscript proposes concrete metrics, CR and MIACR, and a simple C&W/conformal-inspired loss that can be added to training-based unlearning methods.

The experimental section covers multiple unlearning baselines, two datasets/model families, random and class-wise forgetting settings, and reports sensitivity to alpha and calibration size in the appendix.
The limitations and impact sections acknowledge the restriction to image classification and the need for calibration data.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not sound. A conformal prediction set containing the true label for a forget example is not evidence that the model has retained that training example; for random forgetting, a properly retrained model should still generalize to same-distribution forgotten samples. Indeed, the retrain baseline itself has high coverage/CR on forget data, which undercuts the claim that such coverage indicates fake unlearning.

The proposed metrics conflate unlearning with making the model wrong or uncertain on forget samples. This may be appropriate for class removal or harmful-content removal, but it is not generally appropriate for instance-level machine unlearning, where the gold standard is behavior close to retraining on the retain set, not suppression of the true class.

The CPU objective directly pushes the true label outside the conformal set, so improvements in UA/CR are partly by construction and may represent targeted degradation rather than faithful unlearning. Applying this objective to the RT baseline and making it worse as a classifier further illustrates the mismatch with the standard unlearning goal.

The conformal methodology is fragile and not fully justified. CR depends strongly on alpha, calibration distribution, and set-size normalization; the appendix shows pathological behavior such as near-empty sets and even recommends alpha inconsistently, while the main claims rely mostly on alpha=0.05.

The MIA/MIACR setup is underspecified and conceptually unclear: it is not sufficiently explained how conformal prediction is applied to the membership attack, what calibration distribution is used, and why inclusion of the member label in a binary conformal set should be treated as privacy leakage.

The evaluation lacks stronger evidence that the metrics correlate with actual data influence removal, privacy risk, or retraining equivalence. There are no influence-function checks, stronger adaptive attacks, deletion audits, or comparisons to certified/approximate unlearning guarantees.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details and hyperparameters are partly given, but there is no clear code release, exact baseline tuning protocol, or enough detail to ensure fair reproduction of all methods and MIA experiments.
Presentation has several issues, including grammatical errors, confusing notation, inconsistent claims about alpha, and tables whose formatting makes key comparisons hard to verify.

strengths: The paper identifies a real evaluation theme in machine unlearning: point-estimate accuracy and membership attacks can miss information present in model uncertainty or confidence structure.

The authors provide a broad empirical sweep over several unlearning baselines, two datasets/model families, random and class-wise forgetting, and multiple alpha values, with standard deviations in the appendix.
The proposed CPU loss is simple and easy to implement, and the paper includes some useful implementation details such as calibration splits, training epochs, and hardware.
weaknesses: The central premise is not well supported. In split conformal prediction, a correctly calibrated model is expected to include the true label with high probability for unseen in-distribution points. For random forgetting, the exact retrain model should still often classify or cover the forgotten examples because they are drawn from the same distribution. Calling this 'fake unlearning' conflates retained generalization with memorization or failed deletion.

The proposed CR metric is conceptually problematic. It divides coverage by set size, so methods can look better by producing very large, uninformative prediction sets. This pathology appears in the reported Tiny ImageNet results, where Random Label has very large set sizes and extremely low CR, which the limit-based criterion treats as strong forgetting despite poor utility and high uncertainty.

The evaluation criteria are internally inconsistent. The paper says the gap to retraining is desirable, yet also says lower CR on forget data is better. But retraining itself often has high coverage on forget examples in random forgetting, as expected for in-distribution data. The paper does not resolve whether exact unlearning should preserve generalization to forgotten samples or intentionally suppress their true labels.

The CPU framework mainly optimizes the proposed metric by pushing true-label nonconformity above a calibration threshold. This amounts to targeted degradation on the forget samples and does not establish that the resulting model better approximates exact unlearning, removes training influence, or improves privacy beyond the constructed conformal criterion.

The experimental evidence does not convincingly validate the new metrics against a ground-truth notion of unlearning. There is no influence-function, retraining-distance, privacy audit, canary exposure, or data reconstruction evidence showing that CR/MIACR measure deletion rather than calibration or uncertainty artifacts.

The membership conformal metric is underspecified and weakly motivated. It treats membership inference as a binary classifier and then applies conformal sets, but does not clearly describe the attack training/calibration protocol or demonstrate that MIACR corresponds to a stronger privacy guarantee.

Presentation quality is poor in places: duplicated/garbled Figure/Table 1 content, typos, awkward claims such as 'encloses', dense tables that are hard to parse, and overclaims like 'eliminate this issue' without sufficient theoretical or empirical support.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives some hyperparameters, but there is no clear code release statement, many baseline implementation details and MIA protocols are insufficiently specified, and the main tables are difficult to audit.

The limitations section is too narrow. It acknowledges image-only experiments and calibration-data needs, but not the more serious limitations: dependence on calibration quality, distribution shift, metric gaming via large prediction sets, conflict with exact unlearning behavior, and possible utility harm for samples similar to the forget set.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful blind spot in common unlearning evaluations: a forgotten example may be misclassified under UA or missed by a membership classifier while its true label still remains plausible under a conformal prediction set. The empirical demonstration across multiple unlearning methods makes this concern concrete rather than merely rhetorical.

The proposed CR and MIACR metrics are simple, interpretable, and easy to compute given calibration data. They provide a stricter uncertainty-aware view of forgetting and often change the ranking of methods relative to UA/MIA, which is a valuable diagnostic contribution.

The conformal-prediction-based unlearning loss is a natural extension of the metric insight. Results on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT show consistent improvements in forgetting metrics while mostly preserving retain/test accuracy.

The evaluation is broader than many unlearning papers: it includes several baselines, random and class-wise forgetting, different forget fractions, multiple alpha settings, and standard deviations from three trials. The appendix includes useful implementation details, calibration-set discussion, and a limitations/impact statement.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not fully established: inclusion of the true label in a conformal prediction set does not necessarily imply residual memorization or failure to unlearn, since conformal sets are designed to include plausible labels under uncertainty. The paper needs a stronger argument connecting CP-set inclusion specifically to retained training influence, not just model uncertainty or generalizable class knowledge.

CR is somewhat confounded by calibration, accuracy, and set size. Lower CR can be achieved through larger prediction sets or miscalibrated/empty sets, and the paper itself notes sensitivity to alpha and distribution shift. This weakens its status as a standalone forgetting-quality metric.

The proposed CPU loss is only tested on a few training-based methods and relatively small vision settings. There is no evaluation on modern large models, language/generative tasks, or stronger privacy audits beyond the paper’s MIA setup, limiting claims about general machine unlearning.

Ablations are incomplete. It would be important to compare against simpler losses that directly reduce true-label probability, random-label objectives, original C&W-style objectives, or calibration-free variants to isolate the value of conformal thresholding.

Reproducibility is moderate but not complete: hyperparameters and hardware are described, but I did not see a code release, full baseline tuning protocol, or enough detail about the MIA model/procedure to ensure exact replication.

Presentation has noticeable issues: duplicated/garbled text around the introduction and Figure/Table 1, typos such as 'in addiction', dense tables that are hard to parse, and an apparent alpha typo in the appendix recommending 0.5 despite the surrounding discussion favoring small alpha. These do not invalidate the work but reduce clarity.
